data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"For tasks with objectively verifiable outcomes, the non-expert panel-plus-checklist will on average produce more reliable judgments because aggregating independent judgments cancels uncorrelated noise\u2014a structural advantage the single expert cannot replicate internally.","counterconditions":[{"case":"Panelist errors are positively correlated (shared checklist misreading, common training bias) so aggregation cancels far less noise than assumed.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The task's true outcome depends on non-linear cue interactions (SRC_008) that an additive checklist cannot encode, capping panel ceiling below expert ceiling.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The outcome distribution is highly skewed (SRC_006); checklist has high implicit base-rate prior and panel merely tracks base rate, not signal.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"A checklist decomposes the task into atomic, verifiable items. Each non-expert's judgment becomes an independent draw with item-specific noise. Averaging across panelists cancels idiosyncratic errors (Condorcet / measurement theory), leaving the signal. The expert's intuition is a single draw; even if its mean is well-calibrated, its variance on any one case is irreducible. The panel's standard error shrinks as 1/\u221an.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
